title: What are all Spring bean scopes, what is the difference between singleton and prototype, what goes wrong when you inject a prototype into a singleton, and how do you fix it (ObjectProvider, @Lookup, scoped proxy)?
keyPoints: Singleton (default): one instance per ApplicationContext, shared by all injection points and all threads; thread safety is your responsibility.
Prototype: a new instance every time the bean is requested via getBean() or injection; Spring does not manage destruction, so @PreDestroy never runs.
Request scope: one instance per HTTP request, destroyed after the response is sent.
Session scope: one instance per HTTP session, destroyed when the session expires.
The prototype-into-singleton trap: injecting a prototype into a singleton gives the singleton ONE prototype instance forever, completely defeating the scope.
Fix with ObjectProvider<T>: inject a factory and call getObject() per use to get a fresh prototype each time.
Fix with scoped proxy (proxyMode = TARGET_CLASS): a CGLIB proxy delegates to the correct scope's bean on every method call.

s1_definition.oneliner: Singleton means one instance for all; prototype means a new instance every time; injecting a prototype into a singleton gives you ONE prototype forever; fix with ObjectProvider.getObject() to get a fresh instance per use.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Singleton scope** (default) -- one instance per `ApplicationContext`, shared by all injection points and all request threads; eager initialization by default.
- **Prototype scope** -- a new instance created every time the bean is requested; Spring does not manage destruction, so `@PreDestroy` never runs.
- **Request scope** -- one instance per HTTP request; destroyed automatically after the response is sent.
- **Session scope** -- one instance per HTTP session; destroyed when the session expires or is invalidated.
- **Prototype-into-singleton trap** -- injecting a prototype or request-scoped bean into a singleton gives the singleton ONE instance forever because construction happens only once.
- **ObjectProvider<T>** -- the preferred fix: inject a factory that produces a fresh instance on every `getObject()` call.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, the main vault is a singleton: one vault shared by all tellers. A receipt slip is a prototype: a fresh slip for every transaction. A token number is request-scoped: one per customer visit, discarded after the visit. The trap: if the branch manager grabs one receipt slip at the morning meeting and hands it to every customer all day, every customer gets the same receipt number.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Bean Scope Lifetime:

  Singleton:  ═══════════════════════════════════════
              ↑ startup                  shutdown ↓

  Prototype:  ──→ new   ──→ new   ──→ new   (no destroy)

  Request:    ├── req 1 ──┤  ├── req 2 ──┤  ├── req 3 ──┤

  Session:    ├────────── session 1 ──────────┤
              ├────────── session 2 ──────────────────┤

  Prototype-into-Singleton Trap:

  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │  PaymentProcessingService       │
  │  (singleton, created ONCE)      │
  │                                 │
  │  final PaymentTransaction tx    │
  │        ↑                        │
  │  Injected ONCE at construction  │
  │  Same TX for ALL payments!      │
  └─────────────────────────────────┘

  Fix with ObjectProvider:

  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │  PaymentProcessingService       │
  │  (singleton)                    │
  │                                 │
  │  ObjectProvider<TX> provider    │
  │        │                        │
  │  provider.getObject() → new TX  │
  │  provider.getObject() → new TX  │
  │  provider.getObject() → new TX  │
  └─────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Spring bean scopes control the lifecycle and sharing of bean instances. Singleton is the default: one instance shared by all injection points and all request threads, with thread safety being your responsibility. Prototype creates a new instance every time the bean is requested, but Spring does not manage destruction, so @PreDestroy never runs. Request scope creates one instance per HTTP request, and session scope creates one per HTTP session. The most critical pitfall is the prototype-into-singleton trap: injecting a shorter-lived scoped bean directly into a singleton gives the singleton one instance at construction time and keeps it forever, completely defeating the scope.

In the National Bank of India's payment gateway, PaymentTransaction is prototype-scoped because each payment must have its own unique transaction ID, amount, and payment method. The PaymentProcessingService is a singleton. Instead of injecting PaymentTransaction directly (which would give one instance forever), Rajesh injects ObjectProvider of PaymentTransaction. Each processPayment() call invokes provider.getObject(), which asks the container for a fresh prototype. Two concurrent payments from Priya and another customer get completely separate transaction objects with different payment IDs. For per-request data like the trace ID and authenticated user, the team uses a RequestContext bean with @RequestScope, which automatically creates a scoped proxy so the singleton AuditService gets the correct context for each HTTP request.

The key rule is: never inject a shorter-lived bean directly into a longer-lived bean. Use ObjectProvider for prototypes and @RequestScope (which includes proxyMode by default) for request-scoped beans.

Remember one sentence: injecting a prototype into a singleton gives you ONE prototype forever; fix it with ObjectProvider.getObject() to get a fresh instance per use.
